question: In a basic conversation, what is the main job of the person sending the message?

options.A: To evaluate the feedback of the receiver
options.B: To originate and encode the message
options.C: To provide the primary communication channel
options.D: To decode and interpret the message

explanation: The sender is simply the one who starts the talk. They take their thoughts and put them into words or signs to send across! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why is getting feedback from your patient so important in nursing?

options.A: It replaces the need for non-verbal observation entirely
options.B: It confirms whether the patient understood the message
options.C: It dictates the exact medical diagnosis for the patient
options.D: it completely eliminates all environmental noise in the ward

explanation: Feedback is your way of checking in to make sure the patient actually caught what you meant. It keeps everyone on the same page! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is a great example of non-verbal communication?

options.B: Tone of voice and vocal pitch

explanation: Non-verbal means talking without words! Your smile, frown, or how you stand tells a patient a lot before you even open your mouth. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h2)

question: A nurse crosses her arms while listening to a worried patient. How might the patient feel?

options.A: It accelerates the decoding of medical information
options.B: It may project defensiveness and close off the interaction
options.C: It accurately measures the patient's physiological distress
options.D: It helps the patient focus better on verbal instructions

explanation: Body language matters! Crossed arms can accidentally make you look closed off, making it harder for the patient to open up to you. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is the main goal of therapeutic communication in nursing?

options.A: Equal sharing of personal stories between nurse and client
options.B: Fulfilling the social needs of the nursing staff
options.D: The health needs and well-proven goals of the patient

explanation: Unlike chatting with a friend, therapeutic communication is always centered around helping the patient heal and feel supported. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h3)

question: How is nursing communication different from just having a casual friendship with someone?

options.A: Casual friendship relies entirely on structured clinical nursing assessments
options.B: Therapeutic communication gives equal attention to the nurse's personal problems
options.C: Casual friendship is strictly regulated by hospital policies and procedures
options.D: Therapeutic communication maintains professional boundaries focused on patient needs

explanation: We keep professional boundaries so the focus stays entirely on the patient's well-being, keeping the relationship safe and helpful. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which of these is an example of an environmental barrier to good communication?

options.A: Cultural differences in expressing physical pain
options.B: High anxiety levels regarding an upcoming surgery
options.C: Severe hearing impairment in an elderly patient
options.D: Loud monitor alarms and constant staff interruptions

explanation: Environmental barriers are things in the physical surroundings—like annoying hospital noise—that make it hard to hear or talk properly. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h4)

question: A nervous patient is waiting for test results and the nurse says, 'Don't worry, everything is going to be fine.' Why is this a communication trap?

options.A: It uses complex medical jargon that the patient cannot understand
options.B: It forces the patient into a passive physical posture
options.C: It offers false reassurance and dismisses the patient's real fears
options.D: It violates basic environmental safety protocols in the clinic

explanation: Saying 'everything is fine' when you don't know for sure can shut the patient down and make them feel like their worries aren't important. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h4)

question: Which communication technique helps get a patient to open up and share more details?
explanation: Open-ended questions (like 'How are you feeling today?') give patients room to talk freely instead of just giving a quick 'yes' or 'no'. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h5)

question: You need to talk to a patient who speaks a language you do not know. What is the best step to take?

options.A: Obtain a certified professional healthcare interpreter
options.B: Use loud gestures and speak very slowly in English
options.C: Ask a nearby visitor to translate the medical history
options.D: Proceed with the assessment without gathering details

explanation: A professional interpreter is always your best bet to ensure accurate care and protect the patient's privacy. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the best way to talk to an older adult who has a bit of trouble hearing?

options.A: Write down all instructions and avoid speaking altogether
options.B: Shout loudly directly into the patient's ear from behind
options.C: Direct all communication exclusively to the family caregiver
options.D: Speak clearly at a moderate pitch and pace facing the patient

explanation: Face the patient directly and speak calmly and clearly. Shouting or mumbling just makes it harder for them to read your lips and tone! [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h6)

question: A patient with mild dementia is getting confused while trying to fill out admission forms. What should you do?

options.A: Ask the patient to complete the entire form independently
options.B: Break instructions down into short, single-step sentences
options.C: Change the subject and ignore the paperwork entirely
options.D: Speak rapidly to get the admission process finished quickly

explanation: Keep it simple! Giving one short instruction at a time helps prevent overwhelm and keeps the patient calm and involved. [learn more](GNS112_U3_T2#GNS112_U3_T2_h6)
